''fabulatio''(''n''-), story, < ''fabulari'', narrate, < ''fabula'', tale, fable: see ''fable''.] The moral of a fable. ''Bailey''.

'''affabulatory†''' (a-fab′ū-lạ̄-tọ̄-ri), ''a''. Having a moral: as, an ''affabulatory'' allegory. [Rare.]

'''affadyll†''', ''n''. A variant of ''affodill''. See ''daffodil''.

'''affain†''' (a-fān′), ''v. t''. [< ''af''- + ''fain'', an old spelling of ''feign''; with ref. to L. ''affingere'', ''adfingere'', add falsely, < ''ad'', to, + ''fingere'', make, invent, feign: see ''feign''.] To lay to one’s charge falsely or feignedly. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Those errors which are maliciously ''affained'' to him.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Christ. Moderation, p. 35.}}}}

'''affair''' (a̤-fãr′), ''n''. [< ME. ''afere'', ''affere'', < OF. ''afaire'', ''afeire'' (F. ''affaire'' = Pr. ''afar'', ''afaire'' = It. ''affare''), orig. a prep. phrase, ''a faire'' (F. ''à faire'' = It. ''a fare''), to do: ''a'', < L. ''ad'', to; ''faire'' = It. ''fare'', < L. ''facere'', do: see ''fact''. E. ''ado'' is of parallel formation.] '''1.''' Anything done or to be done; that which requires action or effort; a moving interest; business; concern: as, this is an ''affair'' of great moment; a man of ''affairs''; ''affairs'' of state.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy constellation is right apt
For this ''affair''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 4.}}
The nature of our popular institutions requires a numerous magistracy, for whom competent provision must be made, or we may be certain our ''affairs'' will always be committed to improper hands, and experience will teach us that no government costs so much as a bad one.
{{right|''A. Hamilton'', Continentalist, No. 6.}}
Services to those around in the small ''affairs'' of life may be, and often are, of a kind which there is equal pleasure in giving and receiving.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Data of Ethics, § 102.}}}}

'''affamish†''' (a-fam′ish), ''v. t.'' or ''i.'' [< F. ''affamer'', OF. ''afamer'', ''afemer'' = Pr. ''afamar'' = It. ''affamare'', starve, < L. ''ad'', to, + ''famis'', hunger: see ''famish.''] To starve.

'''affamishment†''' (a-fam′ish-mẹnt), ''n.'' The act of starving, or the state of being starved.
{{smaller block|Carried into the wilderness for the ''affamishment'' of his body.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, iv.}}}}

'''affatuate†''' (a-fat̮′ū-āt), ''v. t.'' [< L. as if *''affatuatus'', pp. of *''affatuari'', < ''ad'', to, + ''fatuari'', be foolish. Cf. ''infatuate.''] To infatuate. ''Milton.''

'''affatuate, affatuated''' (a-fat̮′ū-āt, -ā-ted), ''a.'' [< L. *''affatuatus'', pp., after ''infatuate'', ''a.'', q. v.] Infatuated. [Obsolete or poetical.]
{{smaller block|They . . . are so much ''affatuated'', not with his person only, but with his palpable faults, and dote upon his deformities.
{{right|''Milton'', Pref. to Eikonoklastes.}}
<poem>You’ll see a hundred thousand spell-bound hearts
By art of witchcraft so ''affatuate'',
That for his love they’d dress themselves in dowlas
And fight with men of steel.</poem>
{{right|''Sir H. Taylor'', Ph. van Art., II., v. 2.}}}}

'''affear<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' Same as ''afear''.

'''affear<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' Obsolete form of ''affeer''.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|afar|97|affect}}</noinclude>later ''fer'', far. Cf. ''anear''.] '''1.''' From far; from a distance: now usually preceded by ''from''.
{{smaller block|He sawe a place ''afer'' [var. ''a feer'']. {{right|''Wyclif'', Gen. xxii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And ''from a fer'' came walking in the mede.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Good Women, l. 212.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Held ''from afar'', aloft, the immortal prize.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 90.}}}}
'''2.''' Far; far away; at or to a distance; remotely in place: now usually followed by ''off''.
{{smaller block|<poem>''A fer'' fro hem, alle be hem selue.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1215.}}}}
{{smaller block|Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place ''afar off''. {{right|Gen. xxii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The steep where Fame’s proud temple shines ''afar''.</poem>
{{right|''Beattie'', Minstrel, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The coronach stole
Sometimes ''afar'' and sometimes anear.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Dying Swan.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Shakspere uses ''afar off'' also in the sense of remotely in degree; indirectly.
<poem>He that shall speak for her is ''afar off'' guilty,
But that he speaks.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A kind of tender made ''afar off'' by Sir Hugh here.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1.]}}}}

'''afear†''' (a̤-fēr′), ''v. t.''  [Now only E. dial., often shortened to '''''fear''''';  < ME. ''aferen'', < AS. ''āfǣran'', terrify, < ''ā-'' + ''fǣran'' (> ME. ''feren''), terrify, < ''fǣr'', danger, terror, fear: see ''fear''<sup>1</sup>.]  To cause to fear; frighten; terrify; make afraid.
{{smaller block|Clerkes may bere wepen . . . to ''afere'' theues.
{{right|''Dives & Pauper'' (W. de Worde), V. xix. 222. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As ghastly bug does greatly them ''affeare''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iii. 20.}}}}

'''afeard, afeared''' (a-fērd′), ''p. a.''  [< ME. ''afered, aferd,'' p. a.: see ''afear'' and ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>. No connection with ''afraid.'']  Affected with fear; frightened; afraid. [Now colloquial or vulgar.]
{{smaller block|Be not ''afeard''; the isle is full of noises.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 2.}}}}

'''afebrile''' (a-feb′ril), ''a.''  [< Gr. ἀ- priv. (''a-''<sup>18</sup>) + ''febrile.'']  Without fever; feverless.
{{smaller block|The course of subcutaneous fractures without extravasation of blood is usually ''afebrile.''
{{right|''Belfield'', Rel. of Micro-Org. to Disease, p. 38.}}}}

'''Afer''' (ā′fėr), ''n.''  [L., African, used by Milton for ''Africus'' (sc. ''ventus,'' wind), the southwest wind, blowing from Africa; It. ''Affrico'' or ''Gherbino, Garbino.'']  The southwest wind.  ''Milton.''

'''aff''' (ȧf), ''prep.'' and ''adv.'' Off.  [Scotch.]{{smaller|—'''Aff-han′''', offhand; without reserve; frankly.  ''Burns.''—'''Aff hands''', hands off.—'''Aff-loof''', right off from memory, or without premeditation.  ''Burns.''—'''To feeze aff.''' See ''feeze''<sup>5</sup>.}}

'''affa''' (af′ä̤), ''n.''  [The native name.]  A weight, equal to an ounce, used on the Guinea coast. Also spelled ''offa.''

'''affability''' (af-a-bil′i-ti), ''n.''  [< late ME. ''affabylite,'' < OF. ''affabilite,'' F. ''affabilité,'' < L. ''affabilita(t-)s,'' < ''affabilis,'' affable: see ''affable.'']  The quality of being affable; readiness to converse or be addressed; civility in intercourse; ready condescension; benignity.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hearing of her beauty, and her wit,
Her ''affability'', and bashful modesty.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|He had a majestic presence, with much dignity, and at the same time ''affability'' of manner.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 18.}}}}

'''=Syn.''' {{smaller|Sociability, approachableness, accessibility, urbanity, complaisance, suavity, comity, amenity, friendliness, openness.}}

'''affable''' (af′a-bl), ''a.''  [= F. ''affable'', < L. ''affabilis'', ''adfabilis'', easy to be spoken to, < ''affari'', ''adfari'', speak to, address, < ''ad'', to, + ''fari'', speak: see ''fable''.]  '''1.''' Easy of conversation or approach; admitting others to intercourse without reserve; courteous; complaisant; of easy manners; kind or benevolent in manner: now usually applied to those high-placed or in authority: as, an ''affable'' prince.
{{smaller block|An ''affable'' and courteous gentleman.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|He is so insufferably ''affable'' that every man near him would like to give him a beating.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Newcomes, I. xiii.}}}}
'''2.''' Expressing or betokening affability; mild; benign: as, an ''affable'' countenance.
{{smaller block|His manner was very unpretending—too simple to be termed ''affable'': . . . he did not condescend to their society—he seemed glad of it.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xxvii.}}}}

'''=Syn.''' {{smaller|Courteous, civil, complaisant, accessible, mild, benign, condescending, communicative, familiar, easy, gracious, conversable.}}

'''affableness''' (af′a-bl-nes), ''n.'' Affability.

'''affably''' (af′ạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an affable manner; courteously.

'''affabrous†''' (af′a-brus), ''a.''  [< L. ''affaber'', ''adfaber'', skilfully made, < ''ad'', to, + ''faber'', skilful, workmanlike, < ''faber'', workman: see ''fabric''.]  Skilfully made.  ''Bailey''.

'''affabulation†''' (a-fab-ū-lā′shọn), ''n.''  [= F. ''affabulation'', < L. as if *''affabulatio(n-)'', < ''ad'', to, + ''fabulatio''(''n''-), story, < ''fabulari'', narrate, < ''fabula'', tale, fable: see ''fable''.]  The moral of a fable.  ''Bailey''.

'''affabulatory†''' (a-fab′ū-lạ̄-tọ̄-ri), ''a''. Having a moral: as, an ''affabulatory'' allegory. [Rare.]

'''affadyll†''', ''n''. A variant of ''affodill''. See ''daffodil''.

'''affain†''' (a-fān′), ''v. t''.  [< ''af''- + ''fain'', an old spelling of ''feign''; with ref. to L. ''affingere'', ''adfingere'', add falsely, < ''ad'', to, + ''fingere'', make, invent, feign: see ''feign''.]  To lay to one’s charge falsely or feignedly. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Those errors which are maliciously ''affained'' to him.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Christ. Moderation, p. 35.}}}}

'''affair''' (a̤-fãr′), ''n''.  [< ME. ''afere'', ''affere'', < OF. ''afaire'', ''afeire'' (F. ''affaire'' = Pr. ''afar'', ''afaire'' = It. ''affare''), orig. a prep. phrase, ''a faire'' (F. ''à faire'' = It. ''a fare''), to do: ''a'', < L. ''ad'', to; ''faire'' = It. ''fare'', < L. ''facere'', do: see ''fact''. E. ''ado'' is of parallel formation.]  '''1.''' Anything done or to be done; that which requires action or effort; a moving interest; business; concern: as, this is an ''affair'' of great moment; a man of ''affairs''; ''affairs'' of state.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy constellation is right apt
For this ''affair''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|The nature of our popular institutions requires a numerous magistracy, for whom competent provision must be made, or we may be certain our ''affairs'' will always be committed to improper hands, and experience will teach us that no government costs so much as a bad one.
{{right|''A. Hamilton'', Continentalist, No. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|Services to those around in the small ''affairs'' of life may be, and often are, of a kind which there is equal pleasure in giving and receiving.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Data of Ethics, § 102.}}}}

'''2.''' ''pl.'' Matters of interest or concern; particular doings or interests; specifically, pecuniary interests or relations: as, to meddle with a neighbor’s ''affairs''; his ''affairs'' are in an embarrassed state.

{{smaller block|Not I, but my ''affairs'', have made you wait.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 6.}}}}

'''3.''' An event or a performance; a particular action, operation, or proceeding; ''milit.'', a partial or minor engagement or contest; a skirmish: as, when did this ''affair'' happen? an ''affair'' of honor, or of outposts.

{{smaller block|In this little ''affair'' of the advanced posts, I am concerned to add that Lieut. B. was killed.
{{right|''Wellington’s Despatches.''}}}}

'''4.''' A private or personal concern; a special function, business, or duty.

<poem>Oh generous youth! my counsel take,
And warlike acts forbear;
Put on white gloves and lead folks out,
For that is your ''affair''.  ''Lady M. W. Montagu.''</poem>
{{smaller block|To marry a rich foreign nobleman of more than thrice her age was precisely her ''affair''.
{{right|''J. Hawthorne'', Dust, p. 102.}}}}

'''5.''' Thing; matter; concern: applied to anything made or existing, with a descriptive or qualifying term: as, this machine is a complicated ''affair''; his anger is an ''affair'' of no consequence.

{{smaller block|"They are offended," said Kristian Koppig, leaving the house, and wandering up to the little Protestant ''affair'' known as Christ Church.
{{right|''G. W. Cable'', Old Creole Days, p. 231.}}}}

'''6†.''' Endeavor; attempt.

{{smaller block|And with his best ''affair'' obeyed the pleasure of the sun.
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, v. 503.}}}}

'''Affair of honor''', a duel.

'''affamish†''' (a-fam′ish), ''v. t.'' or ''i.''  [< F. ''affamer'', OF. ''afamer'', ''afemer'' = Pr. ''afamar'' = It. ''affamare'', starve, < L. ''ad'', to, + ''famis'', hunger: see ''famish.'']  To starve.

'''affamishment†''' (a-fam′ish-mẹnt), ''n.'' The act of starving, or the state of being starved.
{{smaller block|Carried into the wilderness for the ''affamishment'' of his body.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, iv.}}}}

'''affatuate†''' (a-fat̮′ū-āt), ''v. t.''  [< L. as if *''affatuatus'', pp. of *''affatuari'', < ''ad'', to, + ''fatuari'', be foolish. Cf. ''infatuate.'']  To infatuate.  ''Milton.''

'''affatuate, affatuated''' (a-fat̮′ū-āt, -ā-ted), ''a.''  [< L. *''affatuatus'', pp., after ''infatuate'', ''a.'', q. v.]  Infatuated. [Obsolete or poetical.]
{{smaller block|They . . . are so much ''affatuated'', not with his person only, but with his palpable faults, and dote upon his deformities.
{{right|''Milton'', Pref. to Eikonoklastes.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You’ll see a hundred thousand spell-bound hearts
By art of witchcraft so ''affatuate'',
That for his love they’d dress themselves in dowlas
And fight with men of steel.</poem>
{{right|''Sir H. Taylor'', Ph. van Art., II., v. 2.}}}}

'''affear<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' Same as ''afear''.

'''affear<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' Obsolete form of ''affeer''.

'''affect<sup>1</sup>''' (a-fekt′), ''v.''  [< ME. ''affecten'', < OF. ''affecter'', < L. ''affectare'', ''adfectare'', strive after a thing, aim to do, aspire to, pursue, imitate with dissimulation, feign; also, in pass., be attacked by disease; freq. of ''afficere'', ''adficere'', act upon, influence: see ''affect<sup>2</sup>'', which is nearly allied to ''affect''<sup>1</sup>; the two verbs, with their derivatives, run into each other, and cannot be completely separated.]  '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To aim at; aspire to; endeavor after.
{{smaller block|<poem>In this point charge him home, that he ''affects''
Tyrannical power.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But this proud man ''affects'' imperial sway.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Iliad.}}}}
'''2.''' To use or adopt by preference; choose; prefer; tend toward habitually or naturally.
{{smaller block|<poem>Musing Meditation most ''affects''
The pensive secrecy of desart cell.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 386.}}}}
{{smaller block|The peculiar costume which he ''affected.''
{{right|''Thackeray'', Newcomes, I. 126. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|The drops of every fluid ''affect'' a round figure.
{{right|''Newton'', Opticks.}}}}
'''3.''' To be pleased with; take pleasure in; fancy; like; love.
{{smaller block|<poem>No profit grows where is no pleasure ta’en;—
In brief, sir, study what you most ''affect.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|They [the Koreans] more particularly ''affect'' the flowering shrubs, to a comparative neglect of the annuals.
{{right|''Science'', V. 252.}}}}
{{smaller block|Maria once told me, she did ''affect'' me.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>With two of them at once I am in love
Deeply and equally; the third of them
My silly brother here as much ''affects.''</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', The Blind Beggar.}}}}
'''4.''' To make a show of; put on a pretense of; assume the appearance of; pretend; feign: as, to ''affect'' ignorance.
{{smaller block|I ''affect'' to be intoxicated with sights and suggestions, but I am not intoxicated.
{{right|''Emerson'', Self-reliance.}}}} '''5.''' To use as a model; imitate in any way.
{{smaller block|Spenser, in ''affecting'' the ancients, writ no language.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Discoveries.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nor can he, however laudatory of the masters he ''affected'' in youth, look upon other modern poets except with the complacency felt by one who listens to a stranger’s rude handling of the native tongue.
{{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 402.}}}}
'''6†.''' To resemble; smack of.
{{smaller block|<poem>He hath a trick of Cœur-de-Lion’s face;
The accent of his tongue ''affecteth'' him.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1.}}}}

'''II.'''† ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To incline; be disposed.—'''2.''' To make a show; put on airs; manifest affectation.

'''affect'''<sup>2</sup> (a-fekt′), ''v. t.''  [< L. ''affectus'', pp. of ''afficere'', ''adficere'', act upon, influence, affect, attack with disease, lit. do to, < ''ad'', to, + ''facere'', do, make. Cf. ''affect''<sup>1</sup>.]  '''1.''' To act upon; produce an effect or a change upon; influence; move or touch: as, cold ''affects'' the body; loss ''affects'' our interests.
{{smaller block|There was not a servant in the house whom she did not . . . infinitely ''affect'' with her counsell.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, 1635.}}}}
{{smaller block|On the whole, certain kinds of particles ''affect'' certain parts of the spectrum.
{{right|''Lockyer'', Spect. Anal., p. 142.}}}}
{{smaller block|The whole character and fortune of the individual are ''affected'' by the least inequalities in the culture of the understanding. {{right|''Emerson'', Nature.}}}}
'''2'''†. To urge; incite.  ''Joye.''—'''3'''†. To render liable to a charge of; show to be chargeable with.
{{smaller block|By the civil law, if a dowry with a wife be promised and not paid, the husband is not obliged to allow her alimony. But if her parents shall become insolvent by some misfortune, she shall have alimony, unless you can ''affect'' them with fraud. {{right|''Ayliffe'', Parergon (1726), p. 59.}}}} '''4.''' To assign; allot; apply: now only in the passive.
{{smaller block|One of the domestics was ''affected'' to his especial service.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair, III. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|A considerable number of estates were ''affected'' to the use of the Imperial family under the name of appanages.
{{right|''D. M. Wallace'', Russia, p. 473.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' To work upon; to concern, relate to, interest, bear upon; to melt, soften, subdue, change. ''Affect'' and ''effect'' are sometimes confused. To ''affect'' is to influence, concern; to ''effect'' is to accomplish or bring about.}}

'''affect'''<sup>2</sup>† (a̤-fekt′), ''n.''  [< ME. ''affect'', < L. ''affectus'', ''adfectus'', a state of mind or body produced by some (external) influence, esp. sympathy or love, < ''afficere'', act upon, influence: see ''affect''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'' ''Affect'', ''n.'', like ''affection'', is formally a deriv. of ''affect''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'', but in usage it rests also in part upon ''affect''<sup>1</sup>.]  '''1.''' Affection; passion; sensation; inclination; inward disposition or feeling.
{{smaller block|<poem>My gray-headed senate in the laws
Of strict opinion and severe dispute
Would tie the limits of our free ''affects'',
Like superstitious Jews.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Love’s Sacrifice, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Rachel, I hope I shall not need to urge
The sacred purity of our ''affects''.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Case is Altered, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''affects'' and passions of the heart.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 97.}}}}
'''2.''' State or condition of body; the way in which a thing is affected or disposed.  ''Wiseman'', Surgery.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
